text: k-means is the most widely used clustering algorithm, and for good reason — the idea fits in one sentence and it scales to large datasets. You tell it how many clusters you want, k, and it finds k center points so that every row is close to the center of its own group.

The algorithm in four steps: choose k starting centers, assign every row to its nearest centroid, move each centroid to the mean of rows assigned to it, and repeat until assignments stop changing. Each pass can only lower the total squared distance from rows to their centroids — that total is called inertia, and it's what k-means minimizes.

Notice the catch — the loop settles at a good answer, but not necessarily the best one, because the result depends on where the centroids started. Fitting on our scaled customer data with k-means plus plus initialization gives an inertia of 52.37, settling in just 2 iterations.

The centers come out in scaled units, unreadable on their own — use the scaler to convert them back: 1190.6 and 3.1 visits, 694.6 and 8.9 visits, 297.0 and 2.0 visits, exactly the group profiles from last lesson. predict assigns new customers to the nearest center — someone spending 650 with 8 visits lands in cluster 1, someone spending 250 with 1 visit lands in cluster 2.

A bad start can trap the loop in a poor solution. Forcing purely random starts with a single attempt each, across four seeds: three seeds reach the good inertia of 52.37, but seed 1 gets stuck at 334.76 — six times worse.

scikit-learn's defaults protect you from this. init equals k-means plus plus spreads the starting centroids out intelligently, and n_init reruns the whole algorithm several times, keeping the lowest inertia. Setting n_init explicitly makes your code's intent clear across library versions.
k-means draws straight boundaries between round, similarly sized blobs. Give it two interlocking crescents instead, and it cuts each one in half rather than separating them properly.

The left panel shows the success case on our customer data, with black stars marking the centroids. The right panel shows the failure on crescent-shaped data — each crescent split right across the two clusters. For shapes like these, DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering is the better fit. To recap: k-means minimizes inertia, needs scaled features and a chosen k, and is sensitive to starting points — which k-means++ and n_init address. It assumes round, similar-sized groups.
